plan.chapterName: Anton, Bivens, and Davis. Calculus, 10th Edition, Figure 5.2.17
plan.contextChunk: This figure is part of a worked example asking to find the volume of the solid generated when the region under y = x^2 over [0, 2] is rotated about the line y = -1. The figure contains two linked views. Left (2D): the xy-plane showing the region R bounded above by the parabola y = x^2 and below by the x-axis between x = 0 and x = 2; the axis of revolution y = -1 is drawn as a horizontal red line, with a rotation arrow indicating revolution about it, and a representative washer cross-section at position x is sketched in gray. Right (3D): the resulting solid of revolution shown in perspective, with a visible central hole (from the inner radius of 1) and the parabolic outer surface. The figure illustrates the washer method: at each x, the cross-section is a washer with outer radius x^2 + 1 and inner radius 1, giving area pi((x^2 + 1)^2 - 1^2) = pi(x^4 + 2x^2), and the volume is computed by integrating this expression from 0 to 2.

interactions.label: Generating curve and axis
interactions.teaches: The washer dimensions come from distances to the rotation axis: the outer radius is f(x)-c and the inner radius is 0-c, so changing either the curve or the axis changes every cross-section and reshapes the solid

interactions.label: x-position of washer
interactions.teaches: Sweeping x shows that the volume is built from washers whose area varies along the interval, with area pi((f(x)-c)^2 - (0-c)^2)
Rotating the view reveals that the gray interior is a cylindrical hole and the blue outer boundary is the surface swept out by the curve

demo_steps.title: Middle washer
demo_steps.narration: At x = 1 with f(x)=x^2 and c=-1, the outer radius is 2 and the inner radius is 1. The washer area is pi(2^2 - 1^2) = 3pi.

demo_steps.title: Thin washer near the start
demo_steps.narration: Near x = 0 the curve is close to the x-axis, so the outer and inner radii are nearly equal. The washer has very little area.

demo_steps.title: Large washer at x = 2
demo_steps.narration: At x = 2 the outer radius is 5 while the inner radius remains 1. This large final washer explains the flared end of the solid.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Use one math unit as one world unit for the left graph and for solid radii. Overall scene spans roughly X = -0.5 to 8.0, Y = -6.2 to 4.7, Z = -5.2 to 5.2. Left 2D sketch lies in the plane Z = 0 with origin at world X = 0, Y = 0. The x-axis runs horizontally from X = -0.45 to X = 2.55 at Y = 0, and the y-axis runs vertically from Y = -2.9 to Y = 4.65 at X = 0. The default region is under y=x^2 over x in [0,2], filled light blue #bfe3f0 at about 55% opacity; the boundary curve is saturated blue #20a7df, stroke width visibly heavier than the axes. Draw the cap at x=2 from Y=0 to Y=4 in dark gray/black. The red rotation axis is the horizontal line Y=c=-1, default color #ff5b63, extending from X=-0.45 through the 3D solid to about X=7.6. Place the label y=-1 just left of the y-axis and aligned with the red line. The representative washer in the left sketch is centered at (sampleX,c,0), lies in a plane perpendicular to the x-axis, and is drawn as a vertical gray translucent annulus: default sampleX=1 gives outer radius R=f(1)-c=2 and inner radius r=0-c=1. The 3D solid is translated to the right: use solid local x in [0,2] mapped to world X = 5 + x, with rotation axis along +X at Y=c, Z=0. Default inner radius r=1 is a cylinder; default outer radius R(x)=x^2+1 grows from 1 at X=5 to 5 at X=7. Thus the right end annulus at X=7 has outer radius 5 and inner radius 1. Outer surface color should be pale blue-gray #c8dce5 with gray shading, opacity about 0.5 to 0.65; inner cylinder and end caps gray #bfc3c6 with stronger opacity. Mathematical formulas for the default figure: R(x)=x^2+1, r=1, A(x)=pi((x^2+1)^2-1^2)=pi(x^4+2x^2), and volume V=integral from 0 to 2 of A(x) dx.
interactionPlan.notes: Parse the equation_input fields reactively and show inline parse errors without destroying the previous valid geometry. For the default textbook case assume f(x) is above y=0 and c is below 0; for edited expressions compute displayed radii as signed textbook washer distances R=f(x)-c and r=0-c, and warn if either becomes negative or if the axis crosses the region. Build the solid as parametric surfaces: outer surface (X=5+x, Y=c+R(x)cos theta, Z=R(x)sin theta), inner surface with radius r, plus annular caps at x=0 and x=2. Rebuild or update buffers when the function or axis changes, using at least 96 angular segments and 120 x-samples for smoothness. Keep the left graph, 3D solid, sample washer, radius guides, and numeric readouts synchronized with the x slider.

authoredContext: Find the volume of the solid generated when the region under the curve y = x2 over the interval [0, 2] is rotated about the line y =−1. Solution. First sketch the region and the axis of revolution; then imagine revolving the region about the axis (Figure 5.2.17). At each x in the interval 0 ≤ x ≤ 2, the cross section of the solid perpendicular to the axis y =−1 is a washer with outer radius x2 + 1 and inner radius 1. Since the area of this washer is A(x) = π([x2 + 1] 2 − 12 ) = π(x4 + 2x2 ) it follows by (3) that the volume of the solid is V = ! 2 0 A(x) dx = ! 2 0 π x4 + 2x2_x000b_ dx = π 1 5 x5 + 2 3 x3 _x0010_2 0 = 176π 15

discrepancies: The initial camera view shows the right-hand solid almost end-on as a huge circular disk, while the source shows a side view of the flared solid of revolution.
The left 2D graph, shaded region R, sample washer, and axis labels are tiny and visually buried behind/near the large solid instead of forming a clear left panel.
The right solid appears mostly opaque gray, losing the source's pale blue translucent outer surface and clearly visible gray inner cylinder/washer structure.
The rotation arrow between the 2D region and the 3D solid is much less prominent than in the source.
The sample washer on the left is present but not visually emphasized at the same scale and placement as the source figure.
Several figure labels are technically present but are too small in the rendered composition to match the source's clear textbook annotations.
evaluation.notes: The mathematical washer concept is mostly correct and the interactions are useful, but the default camera, scale, and coloring make the rendered figure look very different from the source.
action_items: Change the initial camera to a side-on orthographic-style view so the 2D graph is readable and the solid appears as the flared side profile shown in the source.
Separate and rescale the left graph and right solid so the solid does not dominate or obscure the graph, washer, labels, and rotation arrow.
Adjust the solid materials so the outer surface is pale blue translucent and the inner cylinder/end washers are gray, matching the source more closely.
Increase the visual prominence of the red y = -1 axis and the central rotation arrow between the panels.
plan_action_items: Specify a textbook-composite orthographic layout rather than a perspective 3D view that can rotate the solid into an end-on disk.

plan.contextChunk: This figure is part of a worked example asking to find the volume of the solid generated when the region under y = x^2 over [0, 2] is rotated about the line y = -1. The figure contains two linked views. Left (2D): the xy-plane showing the region R bounded above by the parabola y = x^2 and below by the x-axis between x = 0 and x = 2; the axis of revolution y = -1 is drawn as a horizontal red line, with a rotation arrow indicating revolution about it, and a representative washer cross-section at position x is sketched in gray. Right (3D): the resulting solid of revolution shown in perspective, with a visible central hole (from the inner radius of 1) and the parabolic outer surface. The figure illustrates the washer method: at each x, the cross-section is a washer with outer radius x^2 + 1 and inner radius 1, giving area pi((x^2 + 1)^2 - 1^2) = pi(x^4 + 2x^2), and the volume is computed by integrating this expression from 0 to 2.

interactions.teaches: The washer dimensions come from distances to the rotation axis: the outer radius is f(x)-c and the inner radius is 0-c, so changing either the curve or the axis changes every cross-section and reshapes the solid

interactions.label: x-position of washer
interactions.teaches: Sweeping x shows that the volume is built from washers whose area varies along the interval, with area pi((f(x)-c)^2 - (0-c)^2)
Rotating the view reveals that the gray interior is a cylindrical hole and the blue outer boundary is the surface swept out by the curve

demo_steps.title: Middle washer
demo_steps.narration: At x = 1 with f(x)=x^2 and c=-1, the outer radius is 2 and the inner radius is 1. The washer area is pi(2^2 - 1^2) = 3pi.

demo_steps.title: Thin washer near the start
demo_steps.narration: Near x = 0 the curve is close to the x-axis, so the outer and inner radii are nearly equal. The washer has very little area.

demo_steps.title: Large washer at x = 2
demo_steps.narration: At x = 2 the outer radius is 5 while the inner radius remains 1. This large final washer explains the flared end of the solid.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Use one math unit as one world unit for the left graph and for solid radii. Overall scene spans roughly X = -0.5 to 8.0, Y = -6.2 to 4.7, Z = -5.2 to 5.2. Left 2D sketch lies in the plane Z = 0 with origin at world X = 0, Y = 0. The x-axis runs horizontally from X = -0.45 to X = 2.55 at Y = 0, and the y-axis runs vertically from Y = -2.9 to Y = 4.65 at X = 0. The default region is under y=x^2 over x in [0,2], filled light blue #bfe3f0 at about 55% opacity; the boundary curve is saturated blue #20a7df, stroke width visibly heavier than the axes. Draw the cap at x=2 from Y=0 to Y=4 in dark gray/black. The red rotation axis is the horizontal line Y=c=-1, default color #ff5b63, extending from X=-0.45 through the 3D solid to about X=7.6. Place the label y=-1 just left of the y-axis and aligned with the red line. The representative washer in the left sketch is centered at (sampleX,c,0), lies in a plane perpendicular to the x-axis, and is drawn as a vertical gray translucent annulus: default sampleX=1 gives outer radius R=f(1)-c=2 and inner radius r=0-c=1. The 3D solid is translated to the right: use solid local x in [0,2] mapped to world X = 5 + x, with rotation axis along +X at Y=c, Z=0. Default inner radius r=1 is a cylinder; default outer radius R(x)=x^2+1 grows from 1 at X=5 to 5 at X=7. Thus the right end annulus at X=7 has outer radius 5 and inner radius 1. Outer surface color should be pale blue-gray #c8dce5 with gray shading, opacity about 0.5 to 0.65; inner cylinder and end caps gray #bfc3c6 with stronger opacity. Mathematical formulas for the default figure: R(x)=x^2+1, r=1, A(x)=pi((x^2+1)^2-1^2)=pi(x^4+2x^2), and volume V=integral from 0 to 2 of A(x) dx.
interactionPlan.notes: Parse the equation_input fields reactively and show inline parse errors without destroying the previous valid geometry. For the default textbook case assume f(x) is above y=0 and c is below 0; for edited expressions compute displayed radii as signed textbook washer distances R=f(x)-c and r=0-c, and warn if either becomes negative or if the axis crosses the region. Build the solid as parametric surfaces: outer surface (X=5+x, Y=c+R(x)cos theta, Z=R(x)sin theta), inner surface with radius r, plus annular caps at x=0 and x=2. Rebuild or update buffers when the function or axis changes, using at least 96 angular segments and 120 x-samples for smoothness. Keep the left graph, 3D solid, sample washer, radius guides, and numeric readouts synchronized with the x slider.
